doc.title: Alicia Olatuja interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 9, 2018

title: Songs with cultural significance and collective aha moments
summary: Asked about a song like 'A Change Is Gonna Come', she discusses 'Everything Must Change' and a piece on trafficking with Billy Childs.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: They have to play. MW: I wanted to ask this question. As you go through your singing career, sometimes without even making a obvious attempt to do it, your music takes on a certain cultural significance. And I wanted to ask you if you have a song in your repertoire that you think already fits this or will you have an aha moment when that moment comes? For instance. It’s 1963 and Sam Cooke sings “A Change is Gonna’ Come.” It may as well be an African-American national anthem.

Right. MW: You know what I’m saying? Everybody knows it. So I was coaching a girl, she was 17 years old, she was singing for an NAACP convention. And me and another one of the coaches said, and it was all going to be older black people. And we said if you sing this song right there won’t be a dry eye in the auditorium. And she rocked the house. So at that moment she absorbed the history of that song. It transferred into her. She realized she wasn’t just singing a melody. You know what I mean? Do you already have a song in your repertoire that’s something of that cultural validity of power or authority, or will you know that aha moment when you got one.

I think it really depends on the audience first of all. I mean you know if you’re singing for a group of children, they’re just, their aha is very different. I think I’ve had several different aha moments singing different pieces. One of the aha moments that I always feel very connected to is when, on, well some of the tunes that we sing have a different impact, but sometimes I actually do an encore. I don’t know if I’ll do one today, because usually it’s whatever the audience wants. But when we do the encore and when I sing in another configuration program called Songs of Freedom, which celebrates songs of Nina Simone, Abbey Lincoln and Joni Mitchell. One of the tunes that I feel really resonates with me today as much as it did when it was written, is “Everything Must Change.” And when I sing that it’s almost a bittersweetness. Because you realize how much has not changed and how much can change. So there’s that hope that we can still move forward but we have to acknowledge where we’re failing in progression. So I feel like that becomes like a very aha type of moment. But in the same sense I feel, like I was just talking to Miles in the band about this today, I did a piece with Billy Childs and it was about human sex trafficking like just a heavy topic but something that you can’t ignore. And we performed it at Michigan State. And when I was learning the piece and watching all these films trying to just get into the mindset, I was like oh God this is just so heartbreaking. I wasn’t thinking about the aha. I was just trying to really make this

authentic for me. But when I performed the piece and I was sitting, performing in front of rows and rows of survivors, as well as the police department that actually specializes in these rescue missions, then the aha moment was there. And that’s because of who was there. You know I think aha moments can be personal, but they can also be a collective experience. And I think the one that I feel like you’re speaking of in particular is the magical aha moments that happen in the collective experience of performance, which is mind-blowing. I think that’s really powerful and it can change both the audience member and the artist.
